pumac-2017-combinatorics-a-07.title: Reduce to two rooks per line, then recurse
pumac-2017-combinatorics-a-07.body:
**Every row and column has exactly two rooks.** A rook in a row with $r$ rooks and a column with $c$ rooks attacks $(r-1)+(c-1)$ rooks, so $(r,c)\in\{(1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\}$. Let $a$ = number of rows with $3$ rooks and $b$ = number with $1$. Since the row counts sum to $16$, $3a+b+2(8-a-b)=16$, so $a=b$; similarly for columns, $a'=b'$. The $3a$ rooks in 3-rows each lie in a 1-column, and every 1-column's rook is in a 3-row, so $b'=3a$; likewise $b=3a'$. Thus $a=b=3a'=3b'=9a$, so $a=0$: all lines have exactly $2$ rooks.

**Counting $0/1$ matrices with all row and column sums $2$.** Fill the board row by row, tracking how many columns still need $2$ rooks ($x$) and how many need $1$ ($y$). Each row picks two columns: both from the $x$ group ($\binom x2$ ways), both from the $y$ group ($\binom y2$), or one of each ($xy$). The resulting recursion, started at $(x,y)=(8,0)$ with $8$ rows, gives
$$N=187\,530\,840$$
(the known sequence $1,0,1,6,90,2040,67950,3110940,187530840$ for $n=0,\dots,8$).

So $N\bmod1000=840$.

**Answer: 840**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-a-07.title: Cycle recursion (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-a-07.body:
Join two rooks when they share a row or column; since each rook has one partner in its row and one in its column, the graph splits into even cycles alternating row/column steps. Let $f(n)$ count $n\times n$ placements of $2n$ rooks with two per row and column. Analysing how the cycle through the first row can be built (the official solution places $n$ non-attacking rooks on the diagonal and adds the rest) leads to the recursion
$$f(n)=\binom n2\left(2f(n-1)+(n-1)f(n-2)\right),\qquad f(0)=1,\ f(1)=0.$$
Then $f(2)=1$, $f(3)=6$, $f(4)=90$, $f(5)=2040$, $f(6)=67950$, $f(7)=3110940$, $f(8)=187530840$, giving remainder $840$. (A brute-force check of the $4\times4$ case over all placements of $8$ rooks also gives $90$.)

**Answer: 840**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-a-08.title: Expected waiting time via overlaps
pumac-2017-combinatorics-a-08.body:
For a fixed pattern $s$ of length $4$ in fair coin flips, the expected waiting time is
$$E[N_s]=\sum_{k:\ s\text{ has a border of length }k}2^k,$$
summing over $k\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that the last $k$ bits of $s$ equal its first $k$ bits ($k=4$ always counts). This is the classic "Conway leading numbers" result; the official solution derives it with generating functions: if $A(z)$ counts strings avoiding $s$ and $B(z)$ counts strings ending with the first occurrence of $s$, then $A(z)+B(z)=1+2zA(z)$ and $z^4A(z)=B(z)\sum_{k\text{ border}}z^{4-k}$, and $E[N_s]=A(\frac12)$.

The $16$ strings fall into four classes:

| strings | borders | $E[N]$ |
|---|---|---|
| $0000,1111$ | $1,2,3,4$ | $2+4+8+16=30$ |
| $0001,0011,0111,1000,1100,1110$ | $4$ | $16$ |
| $0010,0100,0110,1001,1011,1101$ | $1,4$ | $18$ |
| $0101,1010$ | $2,4$ | $20$ |

Average: $\frac{2\cdot30+6\cdot16+6\cdot18+2\cdot20}{16}=\frac{304}{16}=19$.

**Answer: 19**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-a-08.title: Markov chain check
pumac-2017-combinatorics-a-08.body:
For each pattern, track the longest suffix of the bits seen so far that is a prefix of $s$ (states $0$–$3$; state $4$ = found). With $e_j$ the expected number of further bits from state $j$, $e_j=1+\frac12e_{\delta(j,0)}+\frac12e_{\delta(j,1)}$ and $e_4=0$. For $s=0000$: $e_3=1+\frac12e_0$, $e_2=1+\frac12e_3+\frac12e_0$, ..., giving $e_0=30$. Solving these linear systems for all $16$ patterns (by computer) gives the values $30,16,18,20$ above and an average of exactly $19$.

**Answer: 19**
